strengths: Addresses timely and under-explored problem: Safety alignment in LALMs remains largely unexplored; this work fills an important gap
Insightful empirical findings: Clear analysis (Figure 2, Section 3.3) demonstrating why vanilla activation steering fails on audio due to unfavorable distributional properties in early layers
Novel evaluation metric (BRR): Balanced Refusal Rate effectively captures over-refusal on borderline-safe queries, revealing limitations of existing methods invisible to standard benign benchmarks

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets (Figstep, AdvBench, SORRY-Bench, AJailBench, AirBench), models (Qwen2-Audio, Kimi-Audio), evaluation aspects (harmfulness, helpfulness, utility), and ablations
Practical method: Inference-time only, requires no fine-tuning, computationally efficient, and demonstrates low hyperparameter sensitivity
Consistent improvements: SARSteer achieves best or near-best performance across diverse benchmarks while maintaining helpfulness on benign queries
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective visualizations and logical flow; mathematical intuition provided in appendix
weaknesses: Limited experimental scale: Only 100 harmful-safe paired queries used for alignment (from 350 total), and only 2 LALM models evaluated; unclear generalization to other architectures
Artificial data construction: All harmful queries created via TTS synthesis of text; does not reflect natural adversarial audio or diverse real-world deployment scenarios
Insufficient validation of safe-data generation: LLM-based purification of harmful→safe queries lacks human evaluation of semantic equivalence and appropriateness

Incomplete theoretical justification: While local linearization analysis provided, no rigorous justification for why PCA-estimated subspace captures 'safe semantics'; strong linearity assumptions unvalidated
Over-refusal problem incompletely solved: Even with SARSteer, 20-40% refusal on borderline-safe queries persists (Table 2); no discussion of deployment-acceptable thresholds or user studies
Reproducibility concerns: Depends on OpenAI's TTS API, specific LLM evaluator (Mistral-7b), keyword-based refusal detection; no code release mentioned; 100 alignment samples not explicitly released
Evaluation methodology limitations: LLM-as-a-judge evaluated against single model without inter-rater agreement; keyword-based refusal signals are brittle and language-specific
Questionable generalization to text: Appendix B.4 shows minimal/no improvement on text-only LLM (Table 9), raising questions about whether method is truly audio-specific
Limited failure analysis: No discussion of failure modes, adversarial robustness, or which harm categories the method struggles with; no evaluation against sophisticated jailbreaks
Unfair baseline comparison: Baseline methods not originally designed for LALMs; adapted versions may not be optimal implementations

strengths: Clear and compelling motivation with strong empirical analysis (Section 3) demonstrating why vanilla approaches fail to transfer to LALMs—the t-SNE visualizations effectively show the distributional gap between text and audio modalities

Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation framework including multiple benchmarks (Figstep-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio, AJailBench, AdvBench-audio), two independent LALMs, and the introduction of the BRR metric that better captures the safety-utility tradeoff than existing metrics

Valuable dataset construction: paired harmful-safe audio datasets with minimal lexical similarity but different safety implications provide a sharper testbed for evaluating the critical safety-utility tradeoff

Consistent and strong empirical results: achieves top-2 ASR across diverse benchmarks while maintaining highest helpfulness, with robustness demonstrated across model architectures and hyperparameter ranges
Solid ablation studies (Figure 4) convincingly demonstrate both components are necessary, and hyperparameter analysis (Figure 5) shows robustness to sample size n and component number k
Well-motivated technical approach combining text-derived refusal steering with PCA-based safe-space ablation, supported by mathematical intuition (Appendix A.4)
Clear presentation with good logical flow from problem motivation through solution to comprehensive evaluation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Text-derived refusal steering is a straightforward adaptation (difference between harmful+refusal and harmful audio), and PCA-based safe-space decomposition applies existing techniques. The contribution is primarily in combining known methods for LALMs rather than introducing novel techniques
Small alignment dataset (n=100 pairs) may not be representative of the full harmful query distribution, raising concerns about whether learned steering vectors generalize

Methodological concerns with safe query construction: LLM-based purification via DeepSeek-R1 lacks validation of quality; potential for systematic artifacts from uniform instruction format; all audio synthesized via TTS rather than using real speech

Evaluation reliance on LLM-as-judge (Mistral-7b for ASR): no inter-rater reliability assessment, no human evaluation of helpfulness claims, and potential brittleness of matching-based refusal detection (Table 4)

Insufficient theoretical justification for why text-derived refusal directions effectively steer audio activations: while empirically demonstrated, the mechanism remains unclear—assumes text and audio share sufficient activation structure without rigorous justification
Generalization concerns: only 2 LALMs tested; mixed results on pure text-based LLM (Appendix B.4) with unchanged ASR on Figstep suggest limited transferability beyond audio modality

Key design choices lack principled justification: arbitrary selection of k=10 PCA components (though shown robust), choice of 'I cannot assist with that' as default prompt, unclear why PCA over alternative decomposition methods (ICA, NMF)

Potential issues with baseline comparisons: MDSteer baselines show surprisingly poor performance (sometimes massively degrading harmfulness), raising implementation correctness questions; no comparison with other inference-time safety approaches

Theoretical gaps: local linearization assumption (Appendix A.4) may not hold throughout activation space; assumes linear separability of safe/harmful dimensions; no analysis of failure modes or challenging query types
Missing reproducibility details: no code availability mentioned, incomplete LLM evaluation specifications, computational cost of per-layer PCA not discussed

strengths: Addresses important and timely problem of safety alignment for LALMs with limited prior work
Novel empirical insight about fundamental modality-specific distributional gaps (text-audio), well-supported by t-SNE visualizations and quantitative CKA analysis (0.0631 vs 0.6722)
Practical inference-time defense method requiring no fine-tuning, deployable to existing models
Comprehensive evaluation across 6 LALMs with multiple benchmarks (Figstep-audio, AdvBench-audio, SORRY-Bench-audio, AJailBench, AirBench) and clear evaluation methodology
Introduces balanced refusal rate (BRR) metric that properly captures safety-utility tradeoffs on borderline queries, addressing gap in prior evaluation methods
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of both components; hyperparameter robustness analysis; human evaluation with κ=0.811; sample-level validation (Table 18)
Strong empirical results consistently achieving top-2 performance across diverse settings (e.g., 10.80% ASR vs 51.6% baseline on Qwen2-Audio Figstep-audio)
Excellent reproducibility: code/datasets promised, public models, detailed hyperparameters, multiple random seeds (Table 15), comprehensive appendix with 13 sections
weaknesses: Limited theoretical understanding of why text-audio distributional gaps exist; attribution to 'highly processed audio features' (A.8) is superficial; lacks insight into when/why method should/shouldn't work
Synthetic evaluation data via LLM-based purification and TTS introduces potential biases; paired dataset may not represent true safe queries; real-world adversarial audio could behave differently

Requires 100 harmful-safe paired examples during deployment with no guidance on selection/transferability; Figure 5a shows insensitivity only for range 10-100, leaving open questions about n<10 or n>100

ASR evaluation relies on LLM-as-a-judge with documented conservative bias (43 false positives/500=8.6%, B.11); reported ASR are upper bounds; mixing evaluation methods (matching-based RR vs LLM-based ASR) complicates interpretation
Weak generalization to pure LLMs (B.4: ASR unchanged on Figstep) undermines claims of 'modality-agnostic directions'; limits scope of applicability

Incomplete failure mode analysis: SARSteer still achieves 10.8% ASR on Figstep-audio (Qwen2-Audio)—what are systematic properties of remaining harmful queries? Limited robustness analysis against adaptive attacks designed specifically for PCA-based deflation

Method development somewhat incremental: combines existing techniques (activation steering, PCA, refusal prompting); once modality gap is identified, text-derived steering is relatively straightforward

Unfair fine-tuning baseline comparison: RRS (B.6) tested with 100 samples vs. its recommended 1400+ samples; insufficient justification for why inference-time defense is preferred without matching computational budgets
